pages.title: Guard Logs
pages.summary: Inspect recorded Guard decisions by project, action, risk type, and date
pages.body: Review the Guard decisions recorded for your projects. Use structured filters and cursor pagination to investigate a response, compare policy outcomes, or prepare an export without treating the log as a complete record of all application traffic. A useful incident record connects a decision to its project, direction, time, and reason. Guard Logs provides that review surface for requests sent through the Guard; it cannot explain traffic that bypassed it. GET /api/logs Read recorded decisions The API reads the configured event store within the active organization, optionally narrowed to an owned project. Narrow the investigation Filter by action, direction, riskType, from, and to. The response contains logs and nextCursor; reuse the cursor with the same filters. Review retained context The dashboard shows decision metadata and sanitized content. Use Audit Exports for a separate export workflow rather than assuming the list endpoint returns a download. Project and organization scope Read an organization's events or supply projectId to narrow the result. Structured filtering Filter supported decision values, INPUT/OUTPUT/ANALYZE direction, risk type, and time window. Bounded pagination The filter helper clamps page size to 10–100 records, with 50 as the default. Dashboard session Use a signed-in application session with logs:read permission. An x-api-key header does not authenticate this route. GET /api/logs Select the investigation scope Open Guard Logs with a signed-in account. Select the relevant project and choose a date range that includes a known request. Apply a reproducible filter Filter by direction and decision before narrowing by risk type. Record the filter values alongside any incident notes so another reviewer can repeat the query. Locate a known event Send a synthetic request through the project Guard integration, retain the response, and check that its direction, decision, and time appear after persistence completes. Check pagination and exclusions Use Next page when a cursor is returned and confirm the selected project stays unchanged. Do not expect a standalone Memory check or the Firewall inspect preview to appear here. A useful incident record connects a decision to its project, direction, time, and reason. pages.title: Agent Firewall
pages.summary: Evaluate proposed tool actions and review agent policy decisions
pages.body: Evaluate a proposed tool action against supplied permissions, or use the separate agent-action workflow to record decisions and request approval. The Firewall is a policy-evaluation control: your application must enforce the returned decision before executing a tool. An agent's access to email, files, commands, or external APIs creates risks beyond text generation. Checking an action at the tool boundary gives your executor an explicit reason to allow, restrict, hold, or reject it. POST /api/agent-firewall/inspect Inspect a candidate tool call The session-authenticated inspect route evaluates projectId, tool metadata, permission, action, and optional input. It does not execute the tool or persist an action log. Use the execution-boundary workflow The separate POST /api/agent/action/check route uses a project API key and validates an issued passport before loading agent policy. It records decisions; only the later firewall-policy approval branch can create an approval record. Enforce in the caller The executor must stop blocked or unresolved approval cases and apply read-only or sanitized-content restrictions. A returned ALLOW is not a guarantee that the operation is safe. Permission inspection Preview a tool call using an explicit enabled tool and permission record. pages.title: Policy Engine
pages.summary: Configure project Guard modes, detectors, and risk thresholds
pages.body: Configure how a project's Guard handles detected risks. The policy editor supports named modes, detector switches, output handling, custom topics and patterns, and numeric risk thresholds; changes must be validated against representative application traffic. A detection signal and an application decision are different things. Project policy translates those signals into handling appropriate to your environment, while retaining hard security boundaries implemented by the Guard. PUT /api/projects/policy Load the project policy The dashboard loads the selected project's policy; the session API requires policy:manage permission for both reading and writing. Save the complete configuration PUT upserts a ProjectPolicy and supplies defaults for omitted fields. It invalidates the project-policy cache and emits a policy.changed security event. Evaluate actual Guard responses The input and output Guard paths apply the loaded policy. Test the resulting actions rather than assuming a chosen mode disables every hard block. Guard modes MONITOR, BALANCED, and STRICT are the supported mode values. Detector and output controls Configure detector switches, unsafe output handling, and bare-injection handling. Custom restrictions Set topics, domains, patterns, fallback text, grounding preferences, and riskThresholds values from 0–100. Dashboard session Use a signed-in application session with policy:manage permission. An x-api-key header does not authenticate this route. Record its current values before changing detector, output, or custom-rule settings. Save an explicit policy Use the editor or an authorized same-origin application request. Read back the saved values Reopen the policy or retrieve it with GET /api/projects/policy?projectId=… and compare the mode, switches, and thresholds with the intended configuration. Deliveries are signed and processed by a worker with bounded retries; the receiver must verify the signature, tolerate duplicates, and avoid treating a queued event as a confirmed delivery. Event subscriptions Select supported Guard and usage event types rather than subscribing to an invented catch-all stream. pages.summary: Issue project-scoped agent session tokens and validate their permissions
pages.body: Create an agent identity, issue a scoped session passport, and validate proposed actions against its stored policy and status. The passport is an opaque token stored as a hash, not a signed certificate that independently authenticates every tool action. A long-lived project key and a short-lived agent session serve different purposes. Passports provide a narrower session policy and revocation record, but only code paths that validate the passport can enforce it. Issue a scoped token The issuer combines default and requested policy, creates a random passportToken, stores its hash and expiry, and records an ISSUE audit event. Validate and revoke Validate the token, session, tool, and domain before execution. Revoke the passport when the session should no longer be used; callers still need to honor the validation result. Durable identities Agent identities hold type, status, and default policy within a project. Session policy Passports carry allowed, blocked, and approval-required tools, domains, and declared data/memory scopes. Expiry and audit Issuance and validation/revocation workflows maintain session status and passport audit records. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. pages.title: Transaction Escrow
pages.summary: Hold selected agent actions for review without executing the underlying tool
pages.body: Create an escrow record for an action that needs review, then approve, edit, deny, or consume the approved record. Escrow stores a decision workflow; it does not execute payments, send messages, or automatically intercept an agent. Review should occur before an irreversible operation, not after a log entry is written. Escrow provides a place to preserve the proposed action and decision, while your application remains responsible for reviewer authorization and executing only the reviewed action. POST /api/escrow/create Evaluate the proposed transaction Creation checks the proposed action and risk. It may return ALLOW or BLOCK without creating a pending record; reviewable actions receive a transaction ID, token, and expiry. Review the stored payload The dashboard shows pending actions with redacted and safe payloads. Approval, denial, and edit-and-approve routes update the workflow and audit trail. Consume approval before execution The execute endpoint checks workflow state and marks the record EXECUTED. It returns the reviewed action details; the caller performs the actual tool operation separately. Reviewable transactions Capture session, transaction type, tool, action, target, payload, and risk context. Edit-and-approve Rescan a replacement payload before recording approval. Lifecycle audit Record creation, approval, denial, edits, expiry, and workflow execution state. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. POST /api/escrow/create Define the hold boundary Stop your executor before the real operation and create a test escrow transaction. Use trusted reviewer controls; an agent must not approve its own action merely by claiming actorType USER. Connect review to execution Use the dashboard or an authorized backend to resolve the record. Confirm a pending or denied record never triggers the tool and that the transaction and audit entries appear in the escrow workspace. pages.title: Tool Chain
pages.summary: Evaluate submitted tool sequences for compound risk

Tool Chain can identify risky combinations such as sensitive reads followed by external sends; it only sees steps your integration submits. A sequence can introduce risk that is not apparent from one tool call. Keeping the relevant source, destination, and sensitivity context together helps the executor decide whether the next operation should proceed. Evaluate the proposed step The checker loads stored prior steps and evaluates tool, action, sourceType, destinationType, dataSensitivity, and metadata. Persist decisions and findings The route records the step and any findings, returning stepId, decision, riskLevel, findings, and findingIds. Your executor decides whether to run the step. pages.title: Dry-Run Sandbox
pages.summary: Predict action effects without running the proposed operation
pages.body: Submit a proposed tool action for a rule-based dry-run assessment. The service predicts selected effects and stores a simulation record; it does not launch a sandboxed process or reproduce your entire production environment. Pre-execution inspection can surface high-impact operations before they reach a real tool. A simulation remains an estimate based on supplied fields, so a favorable result is one input to authorization, not permission to skip other controls. POST /api/dry-run/simulate Describe the operation Provide sessionId, dryRunType, tool, action, and optional target and simulatedPayload. Infer effects The pure evaluator inspects action text, payload, and metadata for effects such as external recipients, file changes, network commands, or payment activity. Record the simulation The route returns HTTP 201 with dryRunId, predicted effects, findings, risk, and a decision, and persists an AgentDryRun record. Typed simulations Model email, forms, terminal commands, file changes, API calls, payments, packages, database writes, or custom actions. Explicit decisions SAFE_TO_EXECUTE, REQUIRE_APPROVAL, REVIEW, and BLOCK are distinct outcomes. Reviewable history The dashboard shows recent simulations and predicted effects with redacted payloads. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. POST /api/dry-run/simulate Use a synthetic action first Describe a disposable operation without sending it to a real tool. Select the matching dryRunType and include the target and payload the operation would use. Keep simulation separate from execution Call the simulation before the executor. Require any other application policy checks even after SAFE_TO_EXECUTE; pause approval/review outcomes and stop errors. Inspect expected effects Compare a simple synthetic command with an obviously high-impact action. Check the returned effects and exact decision vocabulary rather than testing for an unrelated Guard action such as ALLOW. Verify no external operation ran Confirm the stub executor was never invoked by the simulation call. Match dryRunId to the stored simulation; the API itself does write history even though it does not run the proposed operation. pages.title: Memory Firewall
pages.summary: Check memory content and distinguish evaluation from managed storage
pages.body: Inspect candidate agent memory for known poisoning, secret, and personal-data signals. The check endpoint returns an assessment only; the separate store workflow persists a redacted memory record and assigns an active, review, or quarantined status. Content saved for later sessions can carry instructions that outlive the request in which they appeared. Checking writes and controlling which stored records are read back gives the application a way to limit that persistent attack surface. POST /api/memory/check Assess candidate memory POST /api/memory/check analyzes content and returns decision, riskLevel, reason, safeContent, and findings. It does not store a memory record or persist a check log. Store through the managed path POST /api/memory/store repeats analysis, stores redacted content and its status, and writes findings and MemoryChangeAudit entries. Respect stored status Only approved active records should enter agent context. Your external memory store must implement its own exclusion and review behavior if it does not use the managed retrieval path. Pattern-based assessment Inspect known safety overrides, fabricated permission, tool hijacks, hidden instructions, secrets, and personal data. Managed record status The store route maps BLOCK/QUARANTINE to QUARANTINED and REVIEW to NEEDS_REVIEW. Change evidence Stored writes retain content hashes, findings, and change-audit records. POST /api/memory/check Choose evaluation or storage For your own memory database, call check before writing and enforce its decision yourself. Use store only when you want a managed SoterAI memory record as well. Preserve scope and read controls Send the required agentName and appropriate memoryScope/memoryType. Keep blocked or quarantined content out of future agent context, including caches or replicas outside this service. Validate the non-persistent check Compare a synthetic preference with a known poisoning instruction and inspect the response. Do not look for a new memoryRecordId or dashboard row after /api/memory/check. pages.title: MCP Drift
pages.summary: Compare caller-submitted MCP tool snapshots for risky changes
pages.body: Submit MCP tool definitions over time and compare their descriptions, schemas, endpoints, and inferred capabilities. MCP Drift records differences between the snapshots you provide; it does not poll a server or automatically disable a tool. Tool metadata can change after initial review. Comparing it before the next use can surface new capabilities or suspicious instructions, but only if the integration captures current definitions and acts on findings. POST /api/mcp/tools/snapshot Submit current definitions Send serverName and tools with name, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, and endpoint as available. The route creates an UNKNOWN-trust registry entry if needed. Compare each submitted tool The route hashes metadata, infers capabilities, and compares the latest stored snapshot of the same project/server/tool. Record changes for review New snapshots and drift findings are stored. The response returns serverRiskLevel, existing serverStatus, snapshotsCreated, drifts, and tool risk details. Metadata change detection Compare description, input/output schema, endpoint, and inferred capabilities. Project server registry Track snapshots by project and serverName. Drift history Review recorded changes and recommendations in the MCP Drift dashboard. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. POST /api/mcp/tools/snapshot Capture a reviewed snapshot Fetch tool definitions using your trusted MCP client and submit them with a stable serverName. Keep the original reviewed definitions in your own change-management record. Submit later snapshots deliberately Repeat collection before using changed tools or on a schedule you operate. pages.title: Legal Boundary
pages.summary: Evaluate consent-sensitive browser and computer-use actions
pages.body: Evaluate declared action categories such as login, payment, terms acceptance, form submission, or scraping against consent and risk rules. Legal Boundary returns a control decision; it is not legal advice, regulatory certification, or an independent check of whether an action is lawful. Some actions need explicit user involvement even when an agent can technically perform them. A consent boundary makes that handoff visible before the application changes an account, submits data, or commits a transaction. The route loads the latest enabled project policy, or uses default rule behavior. Evaluate consent rules Rules distinguish blocked domains and bypass attempts from actions requiring approval, review, or human takeover. Payment, credential entry, and legal acceptance receive specific handling. Record and enforce the decision The route stores a LegalBoundaryCheck and returns decision, reason, requiredUserMessage, evidence, and auditId. Your application must pause or hand off the real action. Action categories Classify read-only, login, forms, messaging, payments, bookings, scraping, account changes, terms, and uploads. Human handoff TAKEOVER_REQUIRED is distinct from ASK_APPROVAL, REVIEW, BLOCK, and ALLOW. Decision history Review stored action, consent flag, risk, and reason in the Legal Boundary workspace. pages.title: Evidence Vault
pages.summary: Collect available control evidence and package reviewable JSON reports
pages.body: Collect evidence on demand from selected project records or attach a custom evidence item, then assemble a report. Evidence Vault organizes and hashes available data; it does not certify a framework, prove control effectiveness, or automatically collect every event. An audit needs evidence that can be traced to a control and checked for completeness. A structured package can reduce collection work, but reviewers still need to confirm its sources, coverage, and relevance to the audit period. GET /api/evidence/items Collect evidence explicitly POST /api/evidence/collect accepts a custom item or autoCollect: true with selected evidence types. Automatic collection here is an on-demand snapshot of available database records. Build a report Report generation selects stored evidence by IDs or types and produces a structured summary of controls, statuses, risks, and recommendations. Export for review The report export route returns JSON with a contentHash and marks the report EXPORTED. A hash supports content comparison; it is not a third-party attestation. Control-oriented evidence Organize policy, Guard decisions, redaction, approvals, incidents, RAG, passports, chains, canaries, and other supported evidence types. Reviewable reports Create security-posture, incident-summary, customer-trust, audit-export, or AI-risk-review reports. Content hashing Items and exported reports carry SHA-256 content hashes over sanitized data. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. GET /api/evidence/items Choose the evidence scope Identify the project, controls, and records you intend to review. Collect synthetic/custom evidence first, or request an on-demand automatic snapshot from the intended project. Generate a selected report Retain evidence IDs and select the items for the report. Review warning/failure states and the source records before exporting anything for an auditor or customer. A zero count may also result from an unavailable automatic source query. pages.title: Context Lineage
pages.summary: Register source context and evaluate proposed data transfers
pages.body: Register a source's trust and sensitivity, then evaluate a proposed transfer to a destination. Context Lineage uses explicit source IDs, destination metadata, and content signals; it does not automatically trace every datum through an application. A model or agent may combine information from contexts with different disclosure rules. Evaluating the source and destination together can reveal a risky transfer, provided the integration preserves accurate provenance and enforces the returned decision. POST /api/lineage/flow/check Register a source POST /api/lineage/source/register stores source type, trust, sensitivity, a content hash, and redacted content, and returns sourceId. Check a transfer The flow route loads supplied sourceIds only within the API key's project, then evaluates destination trust, content, and applicable sensitivity rules. Record flow evidence Every valid flow check writes a ContextFlow. Decisions with an incident type and a non-ALLOW outcome also create a LineageIncident. Source registration Keep source trust separate from sensitivity: they use different enum values. Destination-aware decisions Return ALLOW, BLOCK, REDACT, ASK_APPROVAL, or REVIEW with policy matches and safeContent. Flow and incident views Inspect stored source, flow, and incident records in the Lineage workspace. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. POST /api/lineage/flow/check Register the real provenance boundary Register synthetic sources with the intended sourceType, sourceTrustLevel, and sensitivityLevel. Keep returned sourceIds with the data in trusted application context. Check before moving data Submit sourceIds and the actual destination type/trust before the transfer. Stop denied and unresolved review/approval outcomes, and apply safeContent only when the decision permits it. Compare internal and external transfers Test the same synthetic confidential source toward an internal destination and an external one. Compare decision, policyMatches, and any lineageIncidentId without sending real data. Check source completeness Confirm every requested sourceId resolved in the intended project. Missing IDs are not rejected as a complete-set error, so prevent incomplete provenance from silently reducing the check's sensitivity context. pages.title: Blast Radius
pages.summary: Score declared agent capabilities for planning and risk review
pages.body: Estimate relative exposure from the tools, data sources, destinations, memory access, and controls you declare for an agent. Blast Radius is a rule-based planning score, not a measured probability of compromise or a financial loss forecast. Different agents expose different operations and data. Comparing declared capabilities can help prioritize least-privilege changes, but a lower score only describes the submitted model and does not prove that the deployed permissions changed. POST /api/blast-radius/simulate Describe an agent profile Provide agentName and its tools, optional permissions, data sensitivities, destinations, memory access, and policy flags. Apply weighted rules The evaluator matches tool names and declared controls to fixed weights, clamps the score to 0–100, and produces findings and recommendations. Store the latest profile The simulate route upserts AgentRiskProfile by project and agentName. The dashboard sorts stored profiles by score; reusing a name updates that profile. Declared capability model Describe tools, sensitive sources, external destinations, and memory access. Relative risk score Inspect the score, risk level, findings, and suggested control changes. Scenario planning A separate scenario route applies named scenario weights; the base simulation returns an empty scenarioResults array. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. POST /api/blast-radius/simulate Inventory actual permissions Use trusted application configuration to describe the agent rather than relying on the agent's self-report. Include sensitive sources and external destinations that matter to your review. Save and compare a profile Run a simulation with a stable agentName. Retain the original response before resubmitting tightened capabilities, because the stored profile is updated rather than versioned by this route. Check the inputs behind the score Compare the returned findings with your declared tools and controls. A reduction from a changed policy flag is not evidence that the actual deployed control is enabled. Verify the stored profile Open Blast Radius and match the agent name, score, and recommendations to the response. Validate actual tool permissions separately through the executor's tests. pages.summary: Configure recorded-cost budgets and inspect spending signals
pages.body: Configure a monthly budget and record cost transactions for review alongside anomalies and throttle records. The current route is a cost-accounting control plane, not a provider-enforced spending cap; budget accounting must be validated before using it as an enforcement dependency. Unbounded loops and unexpected traffic can create cost risk. A recorded-cost view helps investigate reported activity, but an application also needs actual provider limits and execution controls because this service does not intercept every provider call. These are based on submitted transactions, not independently fetched provider invoices. pages.title: Security Badges
pages.summary: Read public badge metadata and review a project's published status
pages.body: Configure a project's badge and inspect the public status published for its slug. GET /api/badge returns generic JSON metadata; the project-specific status endpoint and embeddable script are separate surfaces, not an SVG or PNG certification seal. A public status can explain that a Guard integration has recorded activity. It must not imply that every application path is protected, that no incident can occur, or that a compliance assessor has certified the system. GET /api/badge Configure publication The signed-in badge workflow controls badgeEnabled and publicName through PATCH /api/projects/badge with badge:manage permission. Read project status GET /api/badge/[slug] returns a public status derived from badge enablement, monthly usage, and recorded recent blocks. Status is cached for 60 seconds. Embed deliberately The dashboard provides a badge.js script and a public security-status link. Review what the script publishes before embedding it on another origin. Public metadata The catalog endpoint exposes badge metadata and supported status names without authentication. Per-project status The slug endpoint publishes bounded activity metadata, not raw Guard logs or customer text. Publication controls The project owner can enable or disable the badge through the authorized dashboard workflow. Public metadata GET /api/badge is public metadata, not a private account or status endpoint. Badge configuration in the dashboard requires a signed-in session. GET /api/badge Review and enable the test badge Open Security Badges for a disposable project, check its public name and enablement, and copy the actual slug rather than guessing a project identifier. Inspect before embedding Open the project's security-status page and inspect the JSON status. Use the deployment's correct badge.js host; a relative script URL on a different website points at that website, not SoterAI. Distinguish generic and project data Confirm /api/badge returns JSON metadata, then request the actual slug endpoint and compare published status with the test project's recorded activity. Check caching and disable behavior After a deliberate test configuration change, allow the documented cache window before comparing status. Confirm the disabled badge reports INACTIVE rather than treating that state as an outage. A public status can explain that a Guard integration has recorded activity. pages.title: Billing
pages.summary: Review subscription, usage, invoice links, and verified payment state
pages.body: Use the signed-in Billing workspace to review your organization subscription, quota usage, invoice links, and plan history. The catalog's diagnostics route is platform-admin-only and reports Razorpay configuration; it is not a customer billing API. A payment UI result and the server's accepted subscription state are not interchangeable. Billing operations must use verified payment events and preserve an auditable record rather than trusting a client-side success message. GET /api/billing/diagnostics Read organization billing data The dashboard loads subscription, recent invoice records, plan history, and project usage context for the active organization. Use the authorized checkout path Checkout requires billing:update permission and server-side plan pricing. The server creates a provider order and verifies payment through the dedicated billing flow. Keep diagnostics restricted GET /api/billing/diagnostics calls requireAdmin and returns configuration state, mode, and warnings. Ordinary project keys and customer sessions are not sufficient. Subscription and quota view Inspect the current organization plan, subscription status, and displayed usage. Invoice and plan history Open a provider-hosted invoice link when one exists and review recent plan changes. Administrative diagnostics Platform administrators can inspect provider configuration without treating it as customer account data. Platform-admin session GET /api/billing/diagnostics requires a signed-in platform administrator. It reports payment-provider configuration, not a customer's plan or invoices. GET /api/billing/diagnostics Review the active organization Open Billing and confirm which organization and project context are displayed. Review the current plan and usage before taking any paid action. Use only the verified billing flow If a plan change is intended, use the dashboard's authorized checkout and provider verification. Do not send a guessed plan-update request with a project key. Check existing billing records without a purchase Compare the subscription state, usage, and invoice links with records already present in the workspace. An unavailable hosted invoice is not a generated PDF download. Separate sandbox from payment verification For an approved test environment, distinguish mock/test orders from live payment state. Confirm accepted server state after the verified flow; this documentation review performs no payment or account mutation. pages.title: Audit Exports
pages.summary: Queue export records and review the current artifact-delivery limitation
pages.body: Request an audit-export job for Guard logs or webhook deliveries and inspect its recorded row count and manifest signature. The current processor marks export metadata READY but does not produce a downloadable file, so this workflow is not yet an end-to-end download service. An audit handoff needs an actual, scoped artifact with verifiable contents. A job identifier or signature field alone is not the export, and a READY label must not be mistaken for successful delivery of a CSV or JSONL file. GET /api/exports Request a bounded export job GET /api/exports accepts organizationId, kind, format, optional dates, and projectId. It checks reports:export, creates a pending export record, and returns HTTP 202. Process available rows The worker reads up to 25,000 matching rows, calculates a manifest signature, and updates status and row count. The query reads oldest-first within the requested range. Review the delivery gap The current job result contains exportId, rows, and signature, not file bytes or a download URL. The dashboard lists recent metadata but does not complete artifact retrieval. Scoped job requests Choose GUARD_LOGS or WEBHOOK_DELIVERIES with organization/project and date filters. Format selection The request schema accepts JSONL or CSV; accepting a format is not proof that a file was generated. Manifest metadata The worker records row count and an HMAC-SHA256 manifest signature for the job. Dashboard session Use a signed-in application session with reports:export permission. An x-api-key header does not authenticate this route. GET /api/exports Confirm the required artifact path Before relying on exports for an audit, ask the deployment owner how a completed file will be retrieved. This implementation currently records export metadata without delivering that file. Use a controlled request scope If evaluating the job workflow, select synthetic records, the intended organization/project, and a narrow date range. GET creates a job, so do not repeatedly open it as if it were a harmless status query. Check queued and processed state separately Confirm the HTTP 202 response, then have an authorized operator check worker completion and compare the row count with the scoped source records. Do not infer completion from request acceptance. Require an actual artifact Attempt retrieval only through an implemented delivery path and verify file contents and integrity before declaring export success. A job identifier or signature field alone is not the export, and a READY label must not be mistaken for successful delivery of a CSV or JSONL file. Review the delivery gap The current job result contains exportId, rows, and signature, not file bytes or a download URL. The dashboard lists recent metadata but does not complete artifact retrieval. Scoped job requests Choose GUARD_LOGS or WEBHOOK_DELIVERIES with organization/project and date filters. Format selection The request schema accepts JSONL or CSV; accepting a format is not proof that a file was generated. Manifest metadata The worker records row count and an HMAC-SHA256 manifest signature for the job. GET /api/exports GET /api/exports requires a signed-in session with reports:export permission. kind is GUARD_LOGS or WEBHOOK_DELIVERIES; format is JSONL or CSV. It is a state-changing job request, not a file response. Requests are limited to 10 per minute per organization/user. Records have a seven-day expiresAt value, but the processor does not serialize a downloadable artifact or return the old X-Manifest-Signature download header. Artifact delivery is incomplete in the reviewed source. Do not promise downloads, scheduled cloud delivery, or a complete external-audit export from this route. The manifest signature covers count, kind, organization, and generation time, not individual row contents. It does not establish row-content integrity, and the worker does not invoke the available serialization helpers. Rows are limited to 25,000 and depend on stored relational records. The job-status endpoint is platform-admin-only; ordinary export permission does not grant access to it. Guard Logs Evidence Vault Security Best Practices

pages.summary: Follow the setup checklist and verify real integration behavior
pages.body: Use the onboarding checklist to organize project, key, first-request, webhook, badge, report, and SDK setup. Progress combines recorded resource counts with saved flags; completion is a workflow aid, not an end-to-end security validation. A checklist makes setup discoverable, but it cannot replace testing the application path that will handle real traffic. Verify authentication, policy decisions, persistence, and failure behavior before relying on a completed progress indicator. POST /api/guard/input Read user setup progress The dashboard loads saved onboarding flags and counts the user's projects, keys, Guard logs, webhooks, enabled badges, and reports. Follow the next action Each item links to a dedicated setup workspace or guide. Resource existence and saved flags determine completion; the SDK step is manually acknowledged. Make a real project Guard request POST /api/guard/input uses x-api-key and the input Guard contract. It is separate from the signed-in PATCH /api/onboarding progress-update route. Persistent checklist Saved progress and resource counts let a user resume setup. Focused destinations Links continue to project, key, webhook, badge, report, and SDK workflows. Integration starting point The first protected request follows the actual Guard API, not a synthetic onboarding response. Project API key Send x-api-key from a trusted backend. The key identifies the project; a dashboard session does not replace it. Keep the key out of browser code and agent prompts. POST /api/guard/input Prepare a project and server key Open Onboarding and follow the project/key steps. Keep the key in a server secret store and use the quickstart for the supported request shape.
